newsitem.title: USA: Crash relatives sue UAL, Boeing.
newsitem.headline: Crash relatives sue UAL, Boeing.

text.p: Relatives of several victims of a 1991 plane crash in Colorado are suing United Airlines and Boeing Co, alleging mishandling of evidence from the crash, a lawyer said on Tuesday.
The Boeing 737 crashed near Colorado Springs on March 3, 1991, killing all 25 passengers and crew.

The suit alleges that mishandling of wreckage from the plane has deprived the relatives of evidence they say would help them to prove their claim that the crash was caused by a faulty rudder. That claim is a key part of a separate wrongful death lawsuit previously filed by relatives in federal court in Denver.
The new suit was filed last week in Superior Court in San Mateo County near San Francisco, Thomas Bacon, a San Francisco attorney representing one of the plaintiffs, said.
Apart from UAL Corp's United Airlines and Boeing, it names as defendants Parker Hannifin Corp, which supplies components to Boeing, and Parker Bertea, Parker's aerospace group.
The lawsuit said that after the crash, some components were removed from the wreckage and taken to a United Airlines facility at San Francisco airport, in San Mateo County.

It alleged that the companies "caused and allowed certain components...to be altered, changed, lost, replaced, or otherwise acted upon, so as to change the essential character of such components as evidence; to thereby spoil and alter such evidence."

It alleged that the companies obliterated important markings critical to establishing the cause of the crash. The plaintiffs said in court documents they did not know whether the alleged mishandling of the evidence was done intentionally or negligently.
The suit, which requests a jury trial, seeks unspecified general, special and punitive damages.
"Those allegations are totally untrue," Boeing spokeswoman Sherry Nebel said of the suit.

A United Airlines spokeswoman said the company denied any wrongdoing, adding that after the accident everything was under the jurisdiction and guidelines of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), which investigates plane crashes.

D.E. Logan, a spokesman for Parker Hannifin, said the company had not yet seen the lawsuit and could not comment on its specific allegations. But he said the company had fully cooperated with the federal investigation of the crash.

Last month, U.S. safety officials called for the speedy installation of modified rudders on the popular Boeing 737 and for new training so pilots could try to combat any sudden, unexpected rudder movement.

The NTSB recommendations stemmed from investigations of at least two 737 accidents including the Colorado Springs crash. The NTSB has said the 737's rudder system could jam in extreme temperatures, but it has not yet determined the causes of the two crashes.
